title: Florence Nightingale at Scutari
text:
In November 1854, during the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale arrived at the British army's Barrack Hospital at Scutari, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, with a group of thirty-eight nurses. She found wounded and sick soldiers lying in filth, without enough beds, blankets, clean linen, food or basic supplies. Many more men were dying of disease than of wounds.

She met resistance from army doctors at first, but she organized. Using private funds, she bought supplies, set up kitchens and a laundry, and insisted on cleanliness. At night she made rounds of the wards with a lamp, which made her famous in Britain.

Deaths remained extremely high through the winter. In March 1855 the government sent a Sanitary Commission, which cleaned out the sewers and improved ventilation, and the death rate fell sharply.

After the war Nightingale worked with the statistician William Farr on the army's records. The analysis showed that most deaths had come from preventable disease caused by poor sanitation. She presented the data in striking diagrams and used them to push for a Royal Commission on army health, which led to lasting reforms in military hospitals and in nursing.
lesson: Measure what is really happening and show it clearly. Good data, honestly read, can force change that pleading cannot.
source: Nightingale's reports and letters; Notes on Matters Affecting the Health of the British Army (1858); Report of the Royal Commission on the Sanitary State of the Army (1858)
caveat: The fall in deaths at Scutari owed more to the Sanitary Commission than to nursing, as Nightingale's own later analysis recognized.
